title: A Call for Control of Frontier AI Models
content:
September 2026
Artificial intelligence is an extremely powerful technology. It has potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen our economies.
At the same time, the rapid development of frontier AI models poses serious risks to safety and security if not appropriately managed.
Recently we have seen capable AI systems circumventing testing safeguards, exploiting vulnerabilities and gaining unauthorized access to real-world systems.
Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks.
To realise AI’s potential, industry, governments and society must act now. We must address these risks and strengthen oversight — without widening the gap between countries in access to the benefits of AI.
AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law.
We therefore welcome the recently launched initiatives that aim to manage the risks related to frontier technologies, and call for:
- Companies to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation, with qualified evaluators granted sufficient access to assess risks.
- Governments and regional organisations to further develop and coordinate common standards, strengthen transparency — including shared reporting of serious safety incidents — and ensure that countries across all regions have access to scientific capacity, expertise and trusted evaluation.
- UN member states to build on existing international mechanisms and explore creating an international institution, able to set standards, enable verification, and convene states when capability thresholds are crossed.
Jonas Gahr Støre, Prime Minister of Norway
Alexander Stubb, President of Finland

report.summary: Twenty-two world leaders signed a joint call for binding oversight of frontier AI, urging companies, governments and the UN to enforce testing, transparency and international coordination.
report.background: The statement, published by the Office of the President of Finland and signed by leaders from Europe, Asia, Africa, the Middle East, North America and Australia, reflects growing alarm that frontier AI capabilities are outpacing governance. Signatories cite recent cases of capable systems circumventing testing safeguards, exploiting vulnerabilities and gaining unauthorised access to real-world systems, echoing warnings from leading scientists and executives. It builds on earlier efforts — the Bletchley and Seoul AI Safety Summits, national AI Safety Institutes, the EU AI Act, and UN advisory work on AI governance — but goes further by naming mandatory pre-deployment testing, shared incident reporting and a possible new international institution. Notably, the coalition spans both Global North and South, framing oversight as a shared global problem rather than a rich-country concern.
key_points: Companies are asked to adopt transparent safety protocols, including mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation. Crucially, qualified external evaluators would be granted sufficient access to model internals and deployment contexts — a shift from today's voluntary, self-reported safety cards toward verifiable third-party audits that companies currently resist on security and IP grounds.

Governments and regional bodies should coordinate common standards, share reporting of serious safety incidents, and ensure every region has access to scientific capacity, expertise and trusted evaluation. This targets a key inequity: without local evaluation capacity, poorer countries become rule-takers, unable to assess the models deployed on their soil or shape the standards applied to them.

UN member states are urged to build on existing mechanisms and explore creating an international institution able to set standards, enable verification, and convene states when capability thresholds are crossed. The threshold trigger is the most novel element — an early-warning mechanism modelled loosely on nuclear or biosecurity regimes, activated by measured capability jumps rather than fixed dates.

The call is framed around human direction, oversight and control, with development and use aligned to international law. That language pushes back on autonomy-first deployment and on arguments that safety governance should remain purely national, positioning AI risk alongside other global security files handled through treaties and multilateral institutions.

The statement remains open for endorsement from other leaders, signalling that this is political momentum-building rather than a binding instrument. The signatory list mixes very different regulatory cultures, suggesting the immediate goal is a broad coalition and agenda-setting before harder negotiations on enforcement begin.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals a likely shift from voluntary commitments to audited compliance: expect demand for independent evaluation firms, model access agreements, incident-reporting pipelines and evidence logs, plus renewed pressure on release schedules for the most capable models. For developers, the practical effect is more scaffolding around frontier training runs — pre-deployment testing, documented evaluations and clearer capability thresholds — while open-weight and smaller labs may face lighter scrutiny. For regular users, the upside is safer, better-tested systems and clearer accountability when things go wrong; the risk is slower releases, higher costs passed downstream, and a fragmented landscape where safety rules differ by region. The bigger question is enforcement: without verification powers, the call remains a norm-setting step rather than a constraint.
report.tools: To follow the safety-evaluation thread, watch METR's task suites for autonomous-capability testing, the UK AI Safety Institute's open-source Inspect framework, Stanford CRFM's HELM, and EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness for standardised benchmarking. For red-teaming, Nvidia's Garak and Microsoft's PyRIT are widely used open-source tools. The AI Incident Database tracks real-world harm reports, while MLCommons and the International AI Safety Report offer reference standards and evidence syntheses for anyone tracking how these proposals become practice.
